headline: The Restaurant & Hospitality Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet guests and staff, give numbers, times and quantities, describe tables, rooms and food, ask questions, make polite requests and ask for help in Spanish, and start Restaurant & Hospitality Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Greet guests and staff and say common restaurant words clearly
lessons.focus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and the written accent; greetings for each time of day

words.note: Spanish vowels are short and pure: e as in 'met', a as in 'father'.
ch sounds like the ch in 'church'.
j sounds like a strong English h: KA-ha.
ll sounds like English y: SEE-ya.
rr is a rolled, trilled r; z sounds like s in Mexico and the US.
The written accent marks the stressed syllable: me-NÚ.
Stress the last syllable: ca-FÉ.
Single r is a quick tap, like dd in 'ladder'. A woman is la mesera.
c before e or i sounds like s: co-SEE-na.
ue sounds like 'weh': KWEN-ta.
Buenos días until noon, buenas tardes until dark, buenas noches after dark.

words.en: Good afternoon, my name is Ana.
Nice to meet you, welcome to the restaurant.
words.note: Say bienvenida to a woman, bienvenidos to a group.
Formal: use with guests and people you don't know.
Informal: use with coworkers.

lessons.speaking: Greet a coworker at the start of the shift, say your name, and say three restaurant words with clear vowels.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say table numbers, times, prices and kitchen amounts like pounds and dozens
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time with a las, and pounds, ounces, dozens and dollars

words.note: US kitchens weigh in pounds: 5 libras de carne.
Una docena de huevos means 12 eggs.
A las 6 y media means at 6:30.
Use son las for every hour except 1: es la 1.
a las + time tells when something happens.
Use de before an amount: es de 85 dólares.

words.en: A bottle of wine costs 40 dollars.
words.es: Una botella de vino cuesta 40 dólares.

lessons.speaking: Tell a cook what time the shift starts and how many pounds of chicken and dozens of eggs the kitchen needs today.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who you are and describe tables, rooms and food as ready, clean, free or cold
lessons.focus: ser for what something is, estar for its condition or location

words.note: Changes with the noun: la mesa está lista.
For a table: taken. For a person: busy.
For tables and rooms that are open for guests.
A woman is la gerente.
ser: who you are. A woman says Soy la gerente.
estar: a condition that can change.

words.en: The restroom is at the back.
words.note: estar for location: where something is.
ser: what something is.

lessons.speaking: Introduce yourself to a new server as the manager and say which tables are free, clean or ready.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Say what the restaurant has, needs and wants, and what the team has to do
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive for restaurant supplies

words.note: Feminine noun that takes el: el agua fría.
In Mexico and the US, limón usually means lime.
In Mexico also called la periquera.

words.en: I need ice for the bar.
There's a table for 6 on the patio.
words.es: Hay una mesa para 6 en el patio.
words.note: hay means there is or there are.

words.en: Would you like water with ice?
words.note: Formal usted, for one guest.

words.en: We have to clean the tables before opening.
words.es: Hay que limpiar las mesas antes de abrir.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: something that must be done.

words.en: I need clean glasses for table 9.
words.es: Necesito vasos limpios para la mesa 9.

lessons.speaking: Tell a server what the dining room needs, like ice, glasses and napkins, and one thing the team has to do before opening.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Say where you are going, what you plan to do, and what you can do
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer for tasks, poder for can

words.note: In US kitchens, the dry storage room.
Many US kitchens also say el walk-in.
Also la habitación.

words.en: I'm going to the storeroom for napkins.
words.es: Voy a la bodega por servilletas.

words.en: We're going to open the patio at 5.
words.es: Vamos a abrir el patio a las 5.
words.note: ir a + infinitive: a plan.
Les for a table of guests; le for one guest.

words.en: I do the schedule on Mondays.
words.note: hacer: hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacen.

words.en: They're going to clean the walk-in cooler.
words.es: Ellos van a limpiar el cuarto frío.

lessons.speaking: Tell a coworker where you are going, what you are going to do before opening, and what you can do to help.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Describe the daily work of your staff with present-tense verbs
lessons.focus: Present tense of regular -ar, -er, -ir verbs for yo, tú, usted, nosotros, ellos

words.note: A woman is la cocinera.
The person or the machine.
Many US bars also say el bartender.
Many US restaurants also say el busser.
A woman is la anfitriona; many US places say la hostess.
A woman is la clienta.
A woman is la huésped.
Common hotel word in Mexico; a man is el recamarero.
A woman is la jefa de cocina.
-ar verbs: trabajo, trabajas, trabaja, trabajamos, trabajan.
Tú between coworkers; usted with guests.

words.en: Do you receive the deliveries in the morning?
words.es: ¿Usted recibe las entregas en la mañana?
words.note: -ir verbs: recibo, recibes, recibe, recibimos, reciben.

words.en: The cooks prepare the staff meal.
words.es: Los cocineros preparan la comida del personal.

words.en: The servers sweep the dining room at closing.
words.es: Los meseros barren el comedor al cerrar.
words.note: -er verbs: barro, barres, barre, barremos, barren.

lessons.speaking: Tell a new hire who works each station and what the team does every day before and after service.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask guests and staff simple questions about people, places, times and amounts
lessons.focus: Question words: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: Agrees with the noun: cuántos platos, cuántas personas.
Two words means why; porque, one word, means because.
Use before es for 'what': ¿Cuál es su nombre?
Many hotels say la tarjeta for a key card.
Ask at the host stand for the party size.

words.en: What would you like to drink?
words.note: Formal, to one guest. Tomar here means to drink.

words.en: When does the fish order arrive?
What's the name for the reservation?
words.es: ¿Cuál es su nombre para la reservación?

lessons.speaking: Ask a guest how many are in the party, the name for the table, and what they would like to drink.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say what is out, what is not ready yet, and what you need more or less of
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos and otro

words.note: Use with no before the verb: no hay nada.
otra with feminine nouns; never say un otro.
Common in US kitchens for a food order; also el pedido.

words.es: No hay más salmón esta noche.
words.note: Tell servers when an item is out (86).

words.en: Nobody leaves without telling the manager.
words.es: Nadie sale sin avisar al gerente.
words.note: Personal a before a person: avisar al gerente.

words.en: Table 4's order hasn't come out yet.
words.es: La orden de la mesa 4 todavía no sale.

words.en: The guest doesn't want anything else.
words.es: El cliente no quiere nada más.
words.note: Double negative is correct: no ... nada.

words.en: There are fewer people today; I don't need another server.
words.es: Hoy hay menos gente; no necesito otro mesero.

words.en: Never leave the walk-in door open.
words.es: Nunca dejen abierta la puerta del cuarto frío.
words.note: dejen: ustedes command to the whole crew.

lessons.speaking: Tell the kitchen what is out tonight, which order is not ready yet, and whether you need another server.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Make polite requests and give simple usted commands to guests and staff
lessons.focus: ¿Puede…? requests and usted commands for everyday restaurant verbs

words.note: Para llevar means to go.
Common in Mexico and the US; also la bandeja.
Also el mandil in Mexico.
Usted command to one guest; to a group say pasen.

words.en: Can you bring the rag and the broom?
words.es: ¿Puede traer el trapo y la escoba?
words.note: ¿Puede...? is a polite way to ask one worker.

words.en: Wash your hands before going into the kitchen.
words.es: Lávese las manos antes de entrar a la cocina.
words.note: Between coworkers, use tú: lávate las manos.

words.en: Be careful, the floor is wet.
words.es: Tenga cuidado, el piso está mojado.

lessons.speaking: Seat a guest politely, ask them to wait or sign the receipt, and ask a busser to bring the rag and the broom.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize cognates and use survival phrases to get help on a busy shift
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad, -ente and survival phrases for getting help

words.note: -ción words match English -tion and are feminine.
Never guess about an allergy: always confirm with the kitchen.
-dad words often match English -ty.
-ente words often match English -ent.
Same word as English, said GLOO-ten.

words.en: I don't understand, can you repeat, please?
How do you say "tray" in Spanish?
One moment, I'm going to ask in the kitchen.
words.es: Un momento, voy a preguntar en la cocina.
words.note: Use this whenever a guest asks about allergies or ingredients.

words.en: I need help in the dining room, please.
words.es: Necesito ayuda en el comedor, por favor.

lessons.speaking: Tell a cook you don't understand, ask them to repeat more slowly, and ask how to say a word in Spanish.
